This article presents a software package (KICA), which automates the analysis of high throughput fluorescent time-series calcium and action potential data. Being based in MATLAB, KICA is most accessible to users with moderate experience with the language. The software package includes several modules to import, process, detect and analyse pulses, as well as perform quality control and report results. The generation of reports in Excel makes KICA especially user-friendly and accessible to those who are less familiar with MATLAB. The additional parallelisation module allows multiple files to be processed together for faster analysis of high throughput data sets. KICA processes signals imported from csv files to reduce noise and correct any baseline drift before calculating the signal-to-noise ratio, detecting pulses for analysis, and calculating parameters typically used to describe Action Potentials (APs) or Calcium Transients (CaTs).

The source code is freely available in a GitHub repository, which includes exemplar data and a user guide. The guide provides some detail on how to use KICA, but this could be improved to aid usability, particularly for users who aren’t familiar with MATLAB. To better understand how the code works with the stimulation parameters, more experimental details would be helpful. For example, when performing batch file analysis, would this only work if the same stimulation protocol was used? 
                This should be clarified. When tested with our own data (using confocal line-scans from primary cardiomyocytes) we found that KICA could not determine the APD 90 and 95 or the fall time unless the pulse threshold was lowered below 95 % of the peak. The method of detecting pulses above a set threshold also seems to cut off the duration of some CaTs, especially where the decay phase is prolonged (e.g. when measured at room temperature). Working around this requires a very low threshold to be set, 
                which should be detailed in the user guide. The automated wavelet-based denoising technique also seems to be inadequate where the sampling rate is higher, and some suggestions on how to modify the code in that case would be welcome. These additions could form part of a troubleshooting section with common problems and their solutions to make KICA more accessible.

The article itself presents limited results. 
                A second figure should be added to provide an example of the CaT analysis to go alongside the existing AP analysis figure. Additional figures could also demonstrate the quality control module for pulse detection. More details on how the exemplar data was collected (stimulation protocol, cell type, dye used, imaging acquisition settings etc.) 
                should be included. This would make it clearer to the user what each input parameter means, as well as how the analysis might be applied to their own data.

Overall, KICA has the potential to provide a reliable, open-source alternative to existing tools. However, there are a few areas in which the communication of KICA’s capabilities could be improved to make it more user-friendly.

The authors report a six‑month cross‑sectional online survey assessing knowledge, attitude, and practice (KAP) regarding hypertension counseling among community pharmacists across all seven emirates in the UAE.                 Figure 1). The questionnaire development, content validation, pilot testing, scoring rules (knowledge 6 items; attitude and practice 9 Likert items each), and statistical methods (t‑tests/ANOVA, simple and stepwise multiple linear regression) are outlined.

Key findings: 70% had “good knowledge”, 46% “positive attitude”, and 51% “good practice”. Knowledge was higher among full‑time vs part‑time pharmacists; attitude was associated with gender and education; practice was associated with counseling volume. Attitude and practice correlated positively (r≈0.24). Detailed results appear in Tables 1–7 (pp.6–13).                         In Methods (p.4), items were “retained if CVR > 0.78” based on Lawshe’s method, with five academic experts. For N=5 experts, the critical CVR is ~0.99, not 0.78; 0.78 applies only to larger panels. Please (a) clarify whether you computed CVR (Lawshe) or item‑level CVI (Lynn/Polit); (b) if CVR was used, recompute with the correct critical value for N=5 (report item‑level CVR and which items would be retained), and (c) update reliability on the full sample (n=114) after any item changes.

                            outcomes in the primary analyses, report effect sizes and 95% CIs, and, if you wish to provide prevalence, use pre‑specified, defensible thresholds (e.g., knowledge ≥80% correct; Likert mean ≥4/5). Provide sensitivity analyses comparing continuous vs thresholded results.
